Battleship Potemkin. Sergei Eisenstein's 1925 Soviet propaganda epic depicting a 1905 naval mutiny against the Tsarist regime. Using revolutionary montage—the collision and juxtaposition of shots to create meaning—it transcends propaganda to become a technical and artistic masterpiece that taught the world how cinema could shape consciousness and emotion through editing alone.

Eisenstein pioneered montage theory. He believed meaning emerges not from individual shots but from their collision. A cut from one image to another creates emotional and intellectual impact. The film's Odessa Steps sequence remains cinema's most famous demonstration of montage power. A baby carriage tumbles down endless steps, intercut with soldiers, horses, and panic. The horror and outrage come through rhythm and editing rather than narrative.

The film is structured as five acts, each representing a stage of revolutionary consciousness: injustice, mutiny, solidarity, repression, and hope. Eisenstein employed visual symbolism throughout. The battleship itself becomes the people's will. The Tsar's portrait torn down manifests revolution. Geometric composition suggests collective order.

Soviet authorities and intellectuals hailed the film, but it faced censorship elsewhere. Western audiences only gradually recognized its artistic achievement beneath its ideology. Eisenstein's theory of montage reshaped cinema language, and his editing principles influenced decades of cinema and advertising. The film remains a technical and aesthetic text studied in film schools worldwide, along with other foundational works of Soviet montage that demonstrated editing as meaning-making.
